t.7.71.1: Having related this to Rāma, the great sage born from a pot began to speak further words within this very tale.
t.7.71.3: Then, at a certain time, in the delightful month of Caitra, the king approached the charming hermitage of Bhārgava.
t.7.71.2: Then, O Kākutstha, that foolish Daṇḍa ruled there for many tens of thousands of years over a kingdom from which every thorn had been removed.
t.7.71.4: There Daṇḍa saw the daughter of Bhārgava, unequalled in beauty on earth and most excellent, wandering in a region of the forest.
t.7.71.5: Seeing her, that utterly foolish one, tormented by the arrows of Anaṅga, approached the maiden in great agitation and spoke these words.
t.7.71.6: Where are you from, O lovely-hipped one, and whose daughter are you, O fair one? Tormented by Anaṅga, I ask you this, O slender-waisted one.
t.7.71.7: But as he, lustful and crazed with infatuation, was speaking thus, Bhārgavī answered the king with these conciliating words.
t.7.71.8: Know, O lord of kings, that she is Arajā by name, the eldest daughter of the divine Bhārgava, whose deeds are unwearied, and that she dwells in the hermitage.
t.7.71.9: My father is your guru, O lord of kings, and you are the disciple of that great-souled one. If angered, that sage of great austerity would bring a very great calamity upon you.
t.7.71.10: Or if you have any purpose to fulfil with me here, by the good path sanctioned by dharma, then ask my father of great splendour for my hand, O best of kings.
t.7.71.11: Otherwise a dreadful consequence would befall you, for in his wrath that father of mine could burn up even the three worlds.
t.7.71.12: To Arajā, who was speaking thus, Daṇḍa, tormented by the arrows of desire and maddened with passion, placed his joined palms upon his head and replied.
t.7.71.13: Show me your favour, O lady of lovely hips; you ought not to let time slip away. For on your account my very life-breaths are being torn apart, O fair-faced one.
t.7.71.14: For once I have won you, let death come, or even the most dreadful sin; accept me, timid one, your devoted lover, who seeks you, utterly overwhelmed.
t.7.71.15: Having spoken thus, the mighty one seized that maiden by force with his arms and, though she struggled, set about to violate her as he pleased.
t.7.71.16: Having committed that exceedingly dreadful and most cruel wrong, Daṇḍa swiftly set out for his peerless city, Madhumanta.
t.7.71.17: Arajā too, weeping and sorely terrified, waits not far from the hermitage for her father, who is like a god.
